reference.source: Miller's Review of Orthopaedics / Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
clinicalPearls: The patella almost always dislocates laterally, often reducing spontaneously on knee extension
The medial patellofemoral ligament is the key soft-tissue restraint and is torn in most first-time dislocations
Predisposing factors include trochlear dysplasia, patella alta, an increased tibial-tubercle-to-trochlear-groove distance and generalised laxity
A haemarthrosis and medial-sided tenderness are typical; a positive apprehension test indicates instability
Osteochondral fragments from the patella or lateral femoral condyle should be actively sought and may need fixation
First-time dislocations without a loose body are usually managed non-operatively with rehabilitation
Recurrent instability may warrant MPFL reconstruction and correction of bony risk factors
reference.pathophysiology: Lateral displacement of the patella from the trochlear groove occurs when the lateral vector on the extensor mechanism overcomes the medial restraints, tearing the medial patellofemoral ligament. Underlying malalignment and dysplasia (shallow trochlea, patella alta, lateralised tubercle) lower the threshold for dislocation and for recurrence, while impaction of the patella against the lateral femoral condyle can shear off osteochondral fragments.
additionalInvestigations: Radiographs including a skyline/axial patellar view
MRI to assess the MPFL, osteochondral injury and trochlear morphology
CT or MRI measurement of tibial-tubercle-to-trochlear-groove distance
Assessment for generalised ligamentous laxity and limb alignment
redFlags: A displaced osteochondral loose body causing mechanical locking
Extensor mechanism disruption preventing straight-leg raise
reference.prognosis: Most first-time dislocations recover with rehabilitation, but recurrence is common in young patients with dysplasia; surgical stabilisation reduces recurrence when anatomical risk factors are addressed.
pitfalls: Missing an osteochondral fragment that requires surgical fixation
Attributing the haemarthrosis to an ACL tear and overlooking a reduced patellar dislocation
Ignoring bony risk factors so that soft-tissue repair alone fails
Failing to check the extensor mechanism for tendon rupture
references: Brukner and Khan's Clinical Sports Medicine
management: Reduce the acute dislocation by gentle knee extension and then protect the joint in a brace with early controlled mobilisation
Manage first-time dislocations without a loose body non-operatively, with physiotherapy targeting quadriceps and vastus medialis obliquus and hip strengthening plus patellar taping or bracing
Operate to fix or remove osteochondral fragments identified after dislocation
Offer medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction for recurrent instability, combined with correction of bony risk factors such as trochleoplasty or tibial-tubercle transfer where indicated
Investigate anatomical predisposition such as trochlear dysplasia, patella alta, and increased tibial-tubercle-to-trochlear-groove distance to guide surgical planning
Refer to orthopaedics and physiotherapy for rehabilitation and follow-up
